| Drystone wall |
| A field boundary wall |
| Material | Local stone |
| Binding | None (gravity and friction) |
A drystone wall is a wall built from stones without any mortar to bind them together. The wall holds its shape through the careful placement of each stone, the weight of the stones above and the friction between them.[1] Drystone walls are common field boundaries in upland areas where stone is plentiful and the soil is thin.
Because the stones are not fixed, a well-built drystone wall can flex slightly as the ground beneath it freezes and thaws, which makes it more durable in cold climates than a rigid mortared wall. Many surviving walls are several hundred years old.[2]
## Construction
[
edit]
A typical field wall is built as two outer faces of carefully fitted stones, with the space between them packed with smaller rubble known as hearting. Large flat through stones are laid across the full width at intervals to tie the two faces together, and the top is finished with a row of upright coping stones.
The wall is usually built with a batter, meaning it is wider at the base than at the top. Wallers use a wooden frame of the wall's profile and string lines to keep the batter consistent along its length.
## Regional styles
[
edit]
Styles vary with the local stone. Walls built of rounded field stones tend to be lower and wider, while walls of flat sedimentary stone can be built taller and with neater faces. Some regions use distinctive coping patterns that allow a practised eye to tell where a wall was built.
- Galloway dykes, with a solid lower half and a loose, see-through upper half
- Cornish hedges, earth-filled walls faced with stone
- Cotswold walls, built of thin limestone slabs
